content:
Intuit has agreed to sell Mailchimp, its email marketing platform, to Italian technology group Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, five years after buying the business for nearly three times as much in the largest deal in its history.

The agreement, announced on Thursday, November 19, will see Bending Spoons pay about $3.31 billion in cash, while Intuit reinvests roughly $368 million of the proceeds in newly issued Bending Spoons shares, according to [Intuit's announcement](https://investors.intuit.com/_assets/_945d8c0e660907b8173cd2f2ddae7eff/intuit/news/2026-11-19_Intuit_Reports_First_Quarter_Results_and_Enters_1331.pdf). The transaction is expected to close in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary conditions. Intuit disclosed the deal in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission the same day.

The sale price is a striking comedown. Intuit acquired Mailchimp in 2021 for about $12 billion, bringing the Atlanta-based email platform into its small-business software portfolio alongside QuickBooks and TurboTax. At the time, the deal was hailed as a way to put marketing tools in front of millions of small firms. Five years on, Intuit is walking away with less than a third of what it paid.

Intuit said the sale would sharpen its focus on AI-powered products for small businesses, and that it planned to use the cash proceeds to repurchase shares, according to [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/commentary/breakingviews/bending-spoons-mailchimp-pounce-tests-its-limits-2026-11-20/). The company announced the deal alongside its fiscal first-quarter results, which beat Wall Street expectations — yet its shares still fell, a sign that investors were more focused on the Mailchimp exit than on the quarter.

The numbers explain why Intuit decided to cut its losses. Mailchimp's revenue slipped about 1 percent to roughly $1.27 billion in fiscal 2026, driven by fewer paying customers, and Intuit forecast revenue of just $1.256 billion to $1.266 billion for fiscal 2027 — essentially flat. Mailchimp has become a drag on a company whose overall revenue rose 12 percent in the most recent quarter, with its growth engine now firmly in AI-assisted tax and accounting products.

There is also a sharp reversal of course. As recently as May 2026, Intuit's management told investors that Mailchimp would generate more value inside Intuit than any outside buyer was likely to pay, given market conditions. Six months later, the company accepted a price that values Mailchimp at a fraction of its 2021 tag. The speed of the U-turn says much about how quickly the market for marketing software has cooled — and about the pressure on Intuit to fund its AI ambitions without carrying a stagnant asset.

For Bending Spoons, the deal is the biggest test yet of its unusual playbook. The Milan-based group, backed by investors including Berkshire Hathaway, has built a portfolio of well-known but faded technology brands — Evernote, WeTransfer, Vimeo and AOL — buying them cheaply, rebuilding them with new teams, technology and pricing, and betting it can revive growth where the previous owners could not. In September it bought Airtable for about a tenth of the collaboration software company's former valuation. Mailchimp, at $3.68 billion, is by far its largest acquisition, and the question is whether a strategy that worked on smaller brands can scale to a business of this size.

Mailchimp itself is no small prize. Founded in 2001, it grew from a side project into one of the world's best-known email marketing brands, serving millions of small businesses and creators who use it to send newsletters, run campaigns and manage customer lists. Its cheerful branding and freemium model made it a fixture of the small-business internet long before Intuit came calling. For those users, the companies said nothing changes for now: the platform keeps operating while the deal awaits approval.

The sale also fits a wider pattern in technology dealmaking. Private equity firms and acquisitive holding companies have been moving in on listed software businesses whose valuations have fallen sharply since the pandemic-era boom, as public-market investors demand profits rather than growth. The [wave of take-private deals](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/tpg-corpay-bill-6-billion-buyout-november-2026) sweeping the sector — including the $6 billion buyout of fintech BILL agreed the same week — shows buyers believe these businesses are worth more out of the spotlight than in it. The [global sell-off in technology shares](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/global-stocks-worst-run-since-2023-ai-selloff-november-2026) this week underlines how fragile confidence in the sector remains.

What happens next will be watched on both sides. Intuit must show that shedding Mailchimp frees it to grow faster in AI, and that the share buybacks funded by the sale are worth more than keeping the business. Bending Spoons must prove that its turnaround formula, honed on brands a fraction of Mailchimp's size, can revive a platform whose revenue has stalled and whose paying customer base is shrinking. If it succeeds, the $3.68 billion price tag will look like a bargain. If it fails, the deal will stand as a reminder that even the most famous names in software can lose most of their value in five years.
summary: Intuit has agreed to sell its email marketing platform Mailchimp to Italy's Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, a steep discount to the roughly $12 billion it paid five years ago, as it sharpens its focus on artificial intelligence.
title: Intuit sells Mailchimp for $3.68 billion, less than a third of what it paid in 2021
